Measured 2026-10-16 through the Go client: `JSON_OBJECT` and `JSON_ARRAY` of a stored row's `BOOL`, `DATE`, `DATETIME`, `TIME` and `TIMESTAMP` gave `true`, `"2017-03-06"`, `"2017-03-06T12:34:56"`, `"12:34:56"` and `"2017-03-06T12:34:56Z"`, and `JSON_SET`, `JSON_ARRAY_APPEND` and `JSON_ARRAY_INSERT` the same, as do literals (`TestBigQueryJSONBuildersOfStoredRows`). |
| A load of several objects from Cloud Storage | **Verified** all or nothing for JSON, CSV and Parquet loads, with `WRITE_TRUNCATE` and `WRITE_APPEND`; **Not implemented** (501) with no Cloud Storage given to the front | `TestBigQueryLoadOfSeveralObjectsIsOneJob` (#1079), official Go client (`GCSReference` with a wildcard and with two URIs, `Loader.WriteDisposition`). BigQuery's load is one job: it loads every object or none. Measured first through the front, on the pinned emulator: the emulator reads a load from Cloud Storage itself one object at a time, each in a transaction of its own, giving only the first the job's `writeDisposition` (its source, `importFromGCS`), so a `NEWLINE_DELIMITED_JSON` load of two objects whose second failed left the table with the first object's rows, its own gone under `WRITE_TRUNCATE` and `WRITE_TRUNCATE_DATA` and kept under `WRITE_APPEND`; a CSV load with columns, read by the front since #944, left the table as it was. Now the front reads every JSON and CSV load from Cloud Storage itself (its `--storage`, the instance's Cloud Storage) and sends the objects to the emulator as one upload, which it loads in one transaction; a Parquet load the front carries out itself, its rows in a scratch table first. Read back: after JSON (with a schema, without one, two URIs), CSV and Parquet loads whose second object fails, with `WRITE_TRUNCATE` and with `WRITE_APPEND`, the table holds its row as before; loads of two good objects load every row. A CSV load with no schema and no autodetect into a table that does not exist is **400** `invalid`, "No schema specified on job or table" (measured before: the emulator answered 500 "nil pointer dereference", which the Go client retried until its deadline). An `AVRO` or `ORC` load is refused by the emulator before anything is written (400 "not support sourceFormat", measured). **501** `notImplemented`: a load of several objects (more than one URI, or a wildcard) with no Cloud Storage given to the front; one of a single object is sent on. Units `TestCloudStorageLoadReportsCounts`, `TestCSVLoadFromCloudStorage`. |
| Loads through a resumable upload | **Verified** | `TestBigQueryAutodetectHeaderAndResumableLoads` (#919): the Go client with `googleapi.ChunkSize(googleapi.MinUploadChunkSize)` (256 KiB chunks; it uses a resumable upload above its chunk size, 16 MiB by default) loads every row of a CSV of over 768 KiB, and a header BigQuery refuses fails that job, which `jobs.list` reports. The emulator does not serve the protocol: it answered the first request with a `Location` of its own listen address, `http://0.0.0.0:9051/…`, which the Go client retried until it gave up (measured), and it takes a chunk only by `PUT`, where the Go client sends `POST` (from its source). Upstream: [goccy/bigquery-emulator#160](https://github.com/goccy/bigquery-emulator/issues/160) (closed) and [#393](https://github.com/goccy/bigquery-emulator/pull/393) (closed unmerged). The front serves the upload itself: it keeps the job and the chunks, in a file in its container, answers each chunk but the last 308 with its `Range` (or 200 with `X-Http-Status-Code-Override: 308`, as the Go client asks), and on the last sends the job and the data to the emulator as one multipart upload through the same checks as any load. The first request is checked for the table ID and schema; an unfinished upload is dropped after 24 hours. Unit `TestResumableUploads`. |
| Loads from Cloud Storage (`gs://` URIs) | **Verified** from the instance's Cloud Storage | `TestBigQueryAutodetectLoadFromCloudStorage` (#919), official Go client for both services: a CSV written to a bucket loads its rows with `autodetect`, and one whose header BigQuery refuses fails the job and leaves no table. Measured first: the emulator, given no `STORAGE_EMULATOR_HOST`, dialled `storage.googleapis.com` for a `gs://` load. CloudBurrow now starts it with `STORAGE_EMULATOR_HOST` set to the in-cluster Cloud Storage server, `http://storage.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local:4443`, so a load reads the instance's own buckets; without Cloud Storage enabled the name does not resolve and the job fails, still offline. A CSV load's objects are read by the front, from the same server (#944, the CSV loads row); other formats by the emulator. Extract jobs to `gs://` write to the same server: the Extract jobs to Cloud Storage row (`TestBigQueryExtractToCloudStorage`, #939). |
| `jobs.list` with `projection=full`: each job's configuration | **Verified** | `TestBigQueryJobListGivesConfigurations` (#958), official Go client (`Client.Jobs`, which asks for `projection=full`, and `Job.Config`). Measured against the pinned emulator over REST: its `jobs.list` gave each job only `jobReference`, `kind`, `statistics` and `status`, whatever the projection, so `Job.Config()` of a listed job was nil; BigQuery's `full` projection "Includes all job data" (the enum's description in the API's discovery document; [jobs.list](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/rest/v2/jobs/list)). The front keeps each job's configuration from the emulator's answer to `jobs.insert`, and reads a job it has not seen (a `jobs.query`'s, whose answer has none, or one made before the front started) once with `jobs.get`; the last 5,000 are kept, and an older one is read again. A query job's and a `jobs.query` script's text read back as the client wrote them (#939). Without `projection=full` no configuration is given, as BigQuery's `minimal` "Does not include the job configuration". The emulator's `jobs.list` also lists every job whatever the request's `maxResults`; the front pages and filters it (#972, row below). Unit `TestJobListGivesConfigurations`. |
| `jobs.list`: order, `maxResults` and `pageToken`, `stateFilter`, `minCreationTime`, `maxCreationTime`, `parentJobId`, `allUsers` | **Verified** | `TestBigQueryJobListPagesAndFilters` (#972), official Go client (`Client.Jobs` with `State`, `MinCreationTime`, `MaxCreationTime`, `ParentJobID`, `AllUsers`, and `iterator.NewPager` pages of two). Measured first against the pinned emulator over REST: `maxResults=2` listed nine jobs, oldest first, with no `nextPageToken`; its handler (`jobsListHandler`) reads none of the request's parameters. BigQuery's list "is sorted in reverse chronological order, by job creation time", pages by `maxResults` and `pageToken`, and filters by `stateFilter`, `minCreationTime` and `maxCreationTime` ("after or at", "before or at", in milliseconds) and `parentJobId` ("If set, show only child jobs of the specified parent. Otherwise, show all top-level jobs") ([jobs.list](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/rest/v2/jobs/list)). The front does each over the whole list, after its own jobs and the job times (#971) are in it: newest first (jobs of one millisecond, newest made first); a page token names the page's last job, so a job made between pages does not move the next page; a job with a `parentJobId` is listed only under it (a script's child jobs, #1353, the row *A script's child jobs*). The queries the front runs itself for its checks (reading a `CREATE TABLE … AS SELECT`'s columns, the resync statements of #955, and the rest) are left out: they are no client's jobs; the last 5,000 are remembered. `allUsers` lists the same jobs: the emulator has one user, so every job is the caller's. A bad `pageToken`, `stateFilter` or creation time is 400 `invalid`. Unit `TestJobListPagesAndFilters`. |
| Job times: `statistics.creationTime`, `startTime`, `endTime` | **Verified** | `TestBigQueryJobTimes` (#971), official Go client (`Job.LastStatus`, `Job.Status`, `Client.Jobs`, `JobStatistics.CreationTime`, `StartTime`, `EndTime`) and the generated client (`google.golang.org/api/bigquery/v2`) for the raw values: an upload, a load from Cloud Storage and a query job. BigQuery gives them "in milliseconds since the epoch" ([JobStatistics](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/rest/v2/Job#JobStatistics)). Measured first: the emulator gave every job it runs its times in seconds (its source: `startTime.Unix()`; milliseconds since bigquery-emulator patch 0013, #1310), so a load from Cloud Storage and a query job read back 1970-01-21, and an upload's job none, the zero time. The front times each `jobs.insert` and `jobs.query` it sends on: creation and start when it received the job, end when the emulator answered; a job answered with no times, or times in seconds, is given those in the `jobs.insert` answer, `jobs.get`, `jobs.cancel` and `jobs.list`. A job the front did not time (made before the front started, or one of more than 5,000 since) has its seconds read as milliseconds. The jobs the front writes itself (#957) keep their own. Times are the cluster's clock (measured 6 ms behind the host's). Unit `TestJobTimesInMilliseconds`. |
| `jobs.insert` with no `jobReference` | **Verified** | `TestBigQueryJobWithoutReference` (#973), the generated client (`Jobs.Insert` of a `Job` with no `JobReference`, which the official Go client always sends): a query job that succeeds and one that fails, a load from Cloud Storage and an upload each come back with a job ID in the request's project, which `jobs.get` finds, and the loads load. Measured first against the pinned emulator: the query jobs and the load from Cloud Storage were answered 500 "runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference", which the client retries. BigQuery's `jobReference` is optional ([Job](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/rest/v2/Job)); the front gives such a job one before anything else reads it: the path's project, a job ID of its own, and the reference's `location` when it gave one (the emulator gives no job a location otherwise). A copy job, with or without a reference, is the emulator's 400 "unspecified job configuration query" (#987). Unit `TestJobWithoutReferenceIsGivenOne`. |
| `jobs.list` of a job the front failed | **Verified** | `TestBigQueryAutodetectHeaderAndResumableLoads` and `TestBigQueryExceptionHandlersRaiseAndCreateOrReplace` (#919, #918): a load, or a script, the front failed after the emulator ran it is listed with the front's `errorResult`; the emulator lists it as it recorded it, `DONE` and succeeded (measured). A job the emulator itself failed is the next row (#934). Unit `TestScriptHandlerRuns` (since #1201 a handler runs; an error no handler catches still fails the script). |
| `jobs.get` and `jobs.list` of a job the emulator failed | **Verified** | `TestBigQueryFailedJobsReadBackFailed` (#934), official Go client (`Job.Status`, `Client.JobFromID`, `Client.Jobs`). Measured against the pinned emulator: it answered a failing query job's `jobs.insert` with `status.errorResult` ("Table not found") and then `jobs.get` of it with `DONE` and no error; and it answered a failing load 400, then `jobs.get` of it the same way, and listed it with no status. BigQuery keeps a job's `errorResult`. The front notes the failure in each `jobs.insert` answer, an `errorResult` or a 400 or 404 (not a 409, which is about an ID another job holds), and `jobs.get`, `jobs.getQueryResults` and `jobs.list` report it; a job that succeeds still reads back succeeded. The failures are kept in the front's memory, the last 1,000; the emulator keeps no state across a restart either. `jobs.query`, which answers a failure with an error and lists no job for it, is unchanged. Unit `TestFailedJobsReadBackFailed`. |
| Where the checks run | **Verified** from the host, from Cloud Run, and from a pod without Cloud Run | The front runs **in the emulator's pod** (#902), a second container from the locally built storage image (`cloudburrow-storage bigquery-front`, the image the in-cluster Cloud Storage server runs, so enabling BigQuery builds it too), and serves the `bigquery` Service's REST port, 9050; the emulator listens on 9051, which the Service does not publish. Every client reaches the emulator through it: the host's tunnel, which the SDKs, `bq` and the console use through `CLOUDBURROW_BIGQUERY_ENDPOINT`, and any pod that dials `bigquery.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local:9050`, the address `env --format kubernetes` prints and Cloud Run revisions and job tasks are given, with or without Cloud Run; that traffic stays in the cluster, so it does not depend on pods reaching the host (#575). `TestAPodDialingTheBigQueryServiceGetsTheFrontWithoutCloudRun`, on an instance without Cloud Run (emulators shard): a one-off pod running the official Go client at that address gets 409 for a dataset that exists, 400 for a hyphenated dataset ID and for a column named twice, and an `invalid` insertErrors entry for a row missing its REQUIRED value, none of them stored, and port 9060 answers; the Service selects the pod, which runs the front. `TestCloudRunRevisionGetsBigQueryRefusalsThroughTheFront` and `TestCloudRunRevisionDialingTheBigQueryServiceGetsTheFront` (run shard): a revision at the injected endpoint, and one that dials the Service itself, get the same four refusals. Until #902 the front was in the host tunnel's guard, and with Cloud Run the Service was routed to it through `cloudburrow-host` (#874, #881); neither is needed now, and nothing BigQuery's is published to pods through the host. The front serves the Storage Read API's port (gRPC, 9060) too since #1032, and the emulator's moves to 9061, which the Service does not publish either (row *Storage Read API of a table whose ID another dataset has*; unit `TestBigQueryManifestPutsTheFrontOnTheServicePort`). **The emulator's own ports refuse every other pod** (#1114): it listens on its pod's loopback alone (`--host=127.0.0.1`), and Kubernetes asks its container's readiness of the front, which dials 9051 and 9061 on loopback (`/cloudburrow/backend-ready`, `internal/frontready`). `TestEmulatorsBehindAFrontRefuseOtherPods`: from another pod, 9051 and 9061 at the BigQuery pod's IP refuse the connection, and 9050 and 9060 accept it. Measured first with the emulator on `0.0.0.0` (its default): from another pod, `CreateReadSession` of a table in a project the instance does not have, sent to 9061, which the front refuses `NOT_FOUND`, crashed the emulator, and every dataset was gone. DML is not checked. |
| Dry run statement type | **Not reliable** | Measured (#698), over REST: a dry run reports `statementType` `SELECT` for a `DELETE` and for a `CREATE TABLE` alike, so it cannot tell a read from a write. |
| Queries through `jobs.insert` | **Leave a dataset behind** | Measured (#698), over REST: each inserted query job creates a dataset named after its job ID to hold the result, and it is listed with the user's own. `jobs.query`, which the Go client's `Query.Read` sends when nothing forces a job, leaves none (`TestConsoleBigQueryDatasetsSchemaAndQuery` checks the dataset list is unchanged after a console query). |
| Creation and modification times of datasets, tables, views and routines | **Verified** (#1310) | `TestBigQueryResourceTimesInMilliseconds`, official Go client: `DatasetMetadata`, `TableMetadata` (a table, after `Table.Update` too, and a view) and `RoutineMetadata` `CreationTime` and `LastModifiedTime`, and a query job's `JobStatistics` `CreationTime`, `StartTime` and `EndTime`, are within a minute of now. BigQuery gives them in milliseconds since the epoch ([Table](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/rest/v2/tables#Table), [Dataset](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/rest/v2/datasets#Dataset)). Measured first (#698, #1310): the emulator wrote a table's and a job's in seconds (`tables.get` answered `"creationTime":"1792085781"`), which the client read as January 1970, and gave a dataset neither. bigquery-emulator patch 0013 gives them in milliseconds and has `datasets.insert` set a dataset's; a table saved in seconds by an earlier engine keeps them. Models are not served, so a model's are not checked. The console shows no times. |
| Emulator environment variable | **None exists** | No official client reads one. `cloudburrow env` exports `CLOUDBURROW_BIGQUERY_ENDPOINT`, which code passes to `option.WithEndpoint`, and `CLOUDSDK_API_ENDPOINT_OVERRIDES_BIGQUERY`, which only bq reads, with the flags in the `bq` row; see configuration.md. |

### State snapshots

`cloudburrow state save <file>` and `state load <file>`, over `POST /admin/state/export` and
`/admin/state/import` on the loopback control port, with the instance's admin token (#553). The archive is a gzipped tar whose first entry
is a versioned `manifest.json`, naming every enabled service as captured or not, with the reason.
A service is captured **record for record from the store it keeps its state in**, so it comes back
exactly: a queue's retry configuration and state, a task's schedule and dispatch count, a disabled
secret version. This holds whichever backend the instance uses: memory, a durable file, or
Kubernetes Secrets for Secret Manager.

| Service | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Cloud Tasks | **Verified** | `TestStateSaveResetLoadRestoresEverything` (CLI, official SDKs, CI instance) and `TestStateRoundTripsTasksSecretsAndProjects`, record-identical in ephemeral and persistent modes |
| Secret Manager | **Verified** | Same tests: every version and payload restored. In CI the backend is Kubernetes Secrets. **The archive holds secret values in plain form**: the CLI warns, and writes it `0600`. |
| Project registry | **Verified** | Same tests: a project created through the console is restored |
| Cloud Scheduler | **Verified** | `TestStateRestoresSchedulerJobs` (CLI, `cloud.google.com/go/scheduler/apiv1`, CI instance): a paused job is saved, reset away and listed back with its schedule, zone, target and next run (#600). `TestStateSaveCapturesSchedulerJobs` checks the store is record-identical and a job created after the save is gone. A job whose next run passed while it was away fires once on the next tick, as after a restart. |
| Cloud Storage | **Verified** | `TestStateRestoresStorage` and `TestStateRestoresVersionsAndHolds`. The state is exported from the storage server's store directly (#511, `builtinStorageSnapshotter`), so a restore fires no notifications: every bucket with all its fields, soft-deleted buckets, every object version (live, noncurrent and soft-deleted) with its generation, metageneration, holds, retention and customTime, notification configurations and undelivered events, IAM policies, sessions and multipart uploads, and the bytes, streamed. A load verifies that every blob hashes to its content address and that every object version's CRC32C matches, before it replaces anything, in one transaction. **HMAC key secrets are excluded**, and the archive says so (`secretsExcluded`): a restored key keeps its metadata and cannot sign. `TestSnapshotRoundTripKeepsVersionsAndHolds`, `TestSnapshotExcludesHMACSecrets`, `TestSnapshotImportVerifiesBytes`, `TestBuiltinStorageSnapshotRoundTrip` (10 MiB, streamed, never held whole in memory). |
| Pub/Sub | **Verified: resources, not messages** | `TestPubSubStateSaveAndLoad` (CLI, official `pubsub/v2` clients, CI instance, #880) and unit `TestPubSubStateRoundTrip` (through the real front, against `pstest`). Google's emulator has no export, so `pubsubSnapshotter` reads through the front with the official client, for every project CloudBurrow knows and every project a call through the front has named: **every schema with every revision** in order, **every topic** as the front returns it (labels, retention, schema settings), **every subscription with every setting** (ack deadline, retention, retained acknowledged messages, filter, ordering, exactly-once, retry and dead-letter policies, expiration policy, labels, push endpoint and attributes; the real endpoint, never the relay's; the expiration policy and labels an update set, which the front keeps and the emulator refuses, #949: unit `TestPubSubStateKeepsUpdatedLabels`), **how long each subscription had been idle**, its expiration clock, and **every snapshot's name and topic**. A load clears those projects' subscriptions, snapshots, topics and schemas and creates the archive's; each subscription reads back as `ListSubscriptions` read it before the save, and one saved 30 hours into a 48-hour ttl is kept 17 hours after the load and gone 2 hours later. **Not kept:** messages (published and unacknowledged, retained after acknowledgement, or in a snapshot's backlog), ack IDs and leases: a loaded subscription starts empty. A loaded snapshot is taken again from a subscription of its topic, so it marks the moment of the load, with a new expire time. A schema revision gets a new revision ID, and a topic's schema settings are pointed at the new IDs. A subscription whose topic was deleted cannot be created again and is left out. The time between a save and a load does not count towards expiration. |
| Cloud Run | **Not captured** | Services are Knative objects in the cluster; redeploy them from their images |
| Cloud KMS | **Not captured** | Key material is not exported. Keys recreated from their definitions get new material, so ciphertext produced before a `state load` cannot be decrypted after it (`TestStateManifestSaysKMSIsNotCaptured`, #388) |
| Cloud SQL (PostgreSQL) | **Verified** | `TestStateRestoresCloudSQL` (CLI, `pgx`, CI instance): a table's rows come back exactly after they were changed, and a database created since the save is gone. Saved with `pg_dump -Fc` for each application database and loaded with `pg_restore --exit-on-error`, both run **inside the server's pod** through the instance's kubeconfig (#311). Nothing is exposed beyond the existing tunnel. The archive holds the dumps and no kubeconfig or cluster credential (`TestPostgresSnapshotArchiveHoldsNoClusterCredential`, and checked on the real archive). Roles are not captured, because the server has only the one it was initialised with. `reset` does not touch PostgreSQL; a load drops and recreates every application database. |
| Cloud SQL for MySQL | **Not captured** | A real MySQL: use `mysqldump` |
| Memorystore | **Not captured** | A real Valkey, and one per created instance: use its own `BGSAVE`, or the append-only file on its volume. The created instances' records (in `<state-dir>/<name>/memorystore` in persistent mode) are not in the archive either |
| Firestore, Datastore, Bigtable, Spanner, BigQuery | **Not captured** | Emulators with no export. All but Datastore are in-memory; Datastore's store, kept on its volume in persistent mode, is not in the archive |

**Load replaces.** Loading resets each captured service to exactly the archive's contents, in one
atomic commit per service, so nothing created since the save survives. **Refused before anything
is touched:** an archive whose manifest version is unknown (`TestARefusedArchiveLoadsNothing`),
one in another format, one that is not an archive, and one holding a service this instance does
not run.

**From the console** (#801): the **Instance** page's **Save state** downloads the archive `state
save` writes, through the same code (`exportStateArchive`), and **Load state** uploads one through
`state load`'s (`importStateArchive`), streamed into the restore without being held in memory. It
is bounded by its own limit of 5 GiB, not the upload limit in Settings, since the archive captures
the whole instance and Save state must load back (#1250); past it the console answers 413, naming
the limit and `cloudburrow state load`, which has no limit (`TestStateLoadIsNotHeldToTheUploadLimit`,
`TestConsoleLoadsTheArchiveItSavedOverTheUploadLimit`). The
entries are byte-identical to what `state save` writes from the same instance, only the
manifest's `created` differing (`TestConsoleInstanceActsThroughTheAdminAPI`); against the CI
instance, a bucket, a secret and a queue saved, reset and loaded from the console are read back
by the official clients (`TestConsoleStateSaveResetLoadRestores`). See the Console table.

| Every snippet in [examples/python.md](examples/python.md) | — | **Verified** | `test_examples.py` runs each block as written |

**Configuration.** Storage and Pub/Sub need nothing but `cloudburrow env`. The Python Storage
client needs the scheme in `STORAGE_EMULATOR_HOST`, which the Go client does not, and `env` exports
the form both accept. Firestore, Datastore, Bigtable and Spanner read their emulator variables,
which the loopback guard checks at session start; each of these tests skips where the instance
does not enable its service. Cloud KMS and BigQuery, like Cloud Tasks and Secret Manager, need an
explicit channel or endpoint. Cloud Tasks and Secret Manager need an explicit plaintext channel (see
[credentials.md](credentials.md#python-clients-for-cloud-tasks-and-secret-manager)).

**Guards.** The suite refuses to run unless `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` is the generated
fixture and default credentials resolve to it. Every connection through Python sockets must be
loopback, which covers the HTTP clients, and so must every gRPC channel target. A violation
fails the whole session even if the test that caused it caught the error. `test_guard.py` proves
both guards by running sessions that break them. gRPC connects from C, which a Python guard
cannot see, so for gRPC it is the channel target that is checked, not the socket.

**Configuration.** Pub/Sub and Firestore need nothing but `cloudburrow env`: the clients read
`PUBSUB_EMULATOR_HOST` and `FIRESTORE_EMULATOR_HOST` and open a plaintext channel, Firestore's
with the emulator's `owner` token as its only credential. **Storage does not work
with `STORAGE_EMULATOR_HOST` as exported.** The Node client uses the variable verbatim as the
JSON API's base URL, so it would need `/storage/v1`. It also uses it as the upload endpoint, which
must not have that path. So unset the variable and pass its value as `apiEndpoint`, as the client's
own source advises: `new Storage({ apiEndpoint: 'http://127.0.0.1:<port>' })`. With a custom
endpoint the client sends no credentials. Cloud Tasks and Secret Manager read no emulator
variable. Pass the endpoint from `CLOUDBURROW_TASKS_ENDPOINT` or
`CLOUDBURROW_SECRETMANAGER_ENDPOINT` as `apiEndpoint` and `port`, with `sslCreds:
grpc.credentials.createInsecure()` (`grpc` from `google-gax`).

**Guards.** `guard.mjs` is loaded with `--import` into every process of the run. It refuses to
start unless `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` is unset or is the generated fixture, and it checks
that application default credentials resolve to that fixture (exit 3). Every TCP connection and
every DNS lookup must be loopback. Node's gRPC (`@grpc/grpc-js`) is JavaScript and connects
through `net` like the HTTP clients do, so, unlike the Python guard, this one sees the gRPC
sockets as well as the HTTP ones. A violation makes the process exit 4, and so fails the run, even
if the test that caused it caught the error. `guard.test.mjs` proves both guards by running
sessions that break them. Each service's tests skip when `cloudburrow env` exports no variable for
that service.

### Cloud SQL is not an emulator

| Capability | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| A real SQL server, locally | **Verified** | PostgreSQL 17.11 in the cluster, digest-pinned, reached with an ordinary driver. A plain `psql` client created a table and inserted rows with nothing of CloudBurrow's involved. |
| Durability | **Verified, measured** | A real database, so it has a volume in persistent mode, as Datastore's emulator and Memorystore's Valkey do; Firestore, Bigtable, Spanner and BigQuery are in-memory. CI's restart probe (#701): `TestCloudSQLRestartSetup` runs alone just before `stop` and leaves a table with a row. After `stop` and `up` in persistent mode, `TestCloudSQLAcrossRestart` reads the row back; brought up again with `--mode ephemeral`, the server has no volume and the table does not exist (`42P01`). |
| Connecting from `cloudburrow env` alone | **Verified** | `TestCloudSQLFromTheExportedPGVariables` (#584): pgx, given only the `PGHOST`, `PGPORT`, `PGUSER`, `PGDATABASE` and `PGSSLMODE` that `env` exported (every other `PG*` variable cleared), and again given `CLOUDBURROW_CLOUDSQL_URL`, connects and runs `SELECT 1`. The host port is fixed at `9019` (`--port-cloudsql`, moved by `--port-base`). |
| MySQL, locally (`cloudsql-mysql`) | **Verified** | `TestCloudSQLMySQLDataPlane` (#297): MySQL 8.4.11, digest-pinned, reached with `go-sql-driver/mysql` from the host and with the `mysql` client from a pod through `cloudsql-mysql.cloudburrow.svc.cluster.local:3306`; `cloudburrow reset` drops every non-system database. A generated per-instance password, exported by `env` and never printed by `status`. |
| MySQL durability | **Verified, measured** | CI reads back a row written before `stop` after `up` in persistent mode, and finds none after `up --mode ephemeral`. |
| MySQL in the console | **Verified** | Cloud SQL's MySQL page (#868): databases, tables, columns and indexes, an SQL editor that reads by default and writes as the application's user in an opt-in, confirmed Read-write mode (#995), and create and drop database, through the console API and in headless Chrome. See "Cloud SQL for MySQL from the console" under Console. |
| The Cloud SQL Admin API: `sql.instances.list`, `sql.instances.get` | **Verified** | `TestSQLAdminInstancesDescribeTheRunningServers` (#1301), official Go client `google.golang.org/api/sqladmin/v1`, on the `sqladmin` port (`9020`, `CLOUDBURROW_SQLADMIN_ENDPOINT`; v1 under `/v1/` and v1beta4 under `/sql/v1beta4/`). Each running server is one instance in every project: `postgres` (`POSTGRES_17`) and `mysql` (`MYSQL_8_4`), `RUNNABLE`, `databaseInstalledVersion` read from the server (`MYSQL_8_4_11`), connection name `{project}:us-central1:{instance}` (CloudBurrow has no regions), and one `PRIMARY` address, `127.0.0.1`. The port is not in the resource, as it is not on Cloud SQL: it is `PGPORT` or `MYSQL_PORT`. An unknown instance is 404. Settings (tier, flags, backups) are fixed placeholders, not configuration. |
| The Cloud SQL Admin API: `sql.databases.insert`, `sql.databases.list`, `sql.databases.get`, `sql.databases.patch`, `sql.databases.update`, `sql.databases.delete` | **Verified** | `TestSQLAdminDatabasesAndUsersAreTheServers` (#1301), on both servers, and through `gcloud sql` (`TestGcloudSQL`, via `gcloud-setup`'s `sql` override) and Terraform (below): each runs `CREATE DATABASE`, `ALTER DATABASE` or `DROP DATABASE` in the server, and is read back from `pg_database` or `information_schema.SCHEMATA` with `pgx` and `go-sql-driver/mysql`; on MySQL the application's user is granted the new database, as the console does. A second insert is 409; the database the server was initialised with is refused 400. A MySQL charset and collation change lands; PostgreSQL fixes a database's encoding at creation, so a change is 501. **Not Cloud SQL's way:** an error is the HTTP answer itself, not a DONE operation carrying it. |
| The Cloud SQL Admin API: `sql.users.insert`, `sql.users.list`, `sql.users.get`, `sql.users.update`, `sql.users.delete` | **Verified** | Same test: `BUILT_IN` users only. PostgreSQL: `CREATE ROLE … LOGIN CREATEDB CREATEROLE`, which connects as itself. **The password is stored but never checked**: the server trusts local connections, as it always has. MySQL: `CREATE USER 'name'@'%'` (or the host given) with every privilege, a password MySQL checks, and after `users.update` only the new one logs in; `root` and `cloudburrow` cannot be deleted. Other user types (IAM) are 501. |
| The Cloud SQL Admin API: `sql.operations.get`, `sql.operations.list` | **Verified** | Same test: every mutation finishes before it answers, so its operation is `DONE`, and `operations.get` and `operations.list` (newest first, by instance) return it. Operations live in memory and are gone after a restart. `sql.operations.cancel` is served for imports and exports (the next rows). |
| The Cloud SQL connector path: `sql.connect.get`, `sql.connect.generateEphemeral` | **Verified** | `TestCloudSQLConnectorDialsBothServers` (#1330), the official Cloud SQL Go connector `cloud.google.com/go/cloudsqlconn` v1.24.0 through its own `pgxv5` and `mysql` drivers, pointed at the Admin API with `cloudsqlconn.WithAdminAPIEndpoint` and nothing else: it dials `{project}:us-central1:postgres` and `…:mysql` and runs `SELECT 1` on both. `connectSettings` returns the instance's server CA (generated locally per instance on first use and kept in the instance directory, so it survives restarts), `127.0.0.1` as the `PRIMARY` address, and a DNS name; `generateEphemeralCert` signs the connector's public key for one hour. A TLS 1.3 listener on `127.0.0.1:3307`, in the `cloudburrow` process, picks the instance by that DNS name, presents a certificate signed by its CA with `project:instance` as its CN, requires the client certificate issued for that project's instance, and forwards to the server. **Port 3307 is fixed**, as it is in every connector, so `--port-base` does not move it and only one instance at a time can serve connectors; on a second, `connectSettings` is 503 saying so. The Auth Proxy binary is not tested. IAM database authentication (an `access_token`) is 501. |
| The Cloud SQL Admin API: `sql.instances.insert`, `sql.instances.patch`, `sql.instances.update`, `sql.instances.delete`, `sql.instances.restart` | **Verified** | `TestCloudSQLInstanceWrites` (#1330), official Go client `google.golang.org/api/sqladmin/v1` and `cloud.google.com/go/cloudsqlconn`, on both engines: `insert` starts a server of its own for the instance (the image and component code of the server `up` runs, a Deployment `sqlinst-<name>`, its own tunnel, CA and connection name), its operation is `DONE` once the server serves, and the connector then dials it and runs `SELECT 1`. `patch` changes labels, the tier (recorded, not sizing anything), deletion protection and a database flag, which the server itself then reports (`SHOW max_connections`, `@@max_connections`); `update` replaces the settings; deletion protection refuses `delete` with 400; `restart` restarts the pod; `delete` removes the server and its volume. `databaseVersion` is `POSTGRES_13` to `POSTGRES_18`, `MYSQL_8_0` or `MYSQL_8_4` (#1381, next row); `MYSQL_5_7` and another version are 501. Also through `gcloud sql instances create`, `describe`, `list` and `delete` (`TestGcloudSQLInstances`) and Terraform `google_sql_database_instance` with a `google_sql_database` in it, plan clean after apply (`TestTerraformSQLDatabaseInstance`), and the console (`TestConsoleCloudSQLInstancesCreateRestartAndDelete`). The instances `up` runs (`postgres`, `mysql`) refuse a patch, restart or delete with 400 naming the `--services` flag. In persistent mode a created instance and its data survive `stop` and `up`. See [cloudsql.md](cloudsql.md#creating-instances-1330). |
| The Cloud SQL Admin API's read replicas: `sql.instances.insert` with `masterInstanceName`, `sql.instances.promoteReplica`, `sql.instances.stopReplica`, `sql.instances.startReplica` | **Verified** | `TestCloudSQLReadReplicas` (#1330), official Go client `google.golang.org/api/sqladmin/v1` and `cloud.google.com/go/cloudsqlconn`, on both engines: a replica of a created primary is a server of its own replicating by the engine's own replication (PostgreSQL streaming from a `pg_basebackup` as `cloudsqlreplica`; MySQL GTID replication after the primary's GTIDs are turned on online). A row written on the primary is read on the replica through the connector; a write on the replica is refused by its server; the primary answers `replicaNames` and refuses `delete` while it has the replica; the replica answers `READ_REPLICA_INSTANCE` and `masterInstanceName`; `stopReplica` sets `databaseReplicationEnabled` false and `startReplica` resumes; `promoteReplica` makes it a primary that takes writes. A replica of a server `up` runs (`postgres`, `mysql`) becomes RUNNABLE and is listed in its `replicaNames`, the PostgreSQL one a hot standby (`TestCloudSQLReplicaOfUpsServer`). Also through `gcloud sql instances create --master-instance-name`, `describe` and `promote-replica` (`TestGcloudSQLReadReplica`, gcloud 586.0.0) and the console's Create read replica, Stop and Start replication and Promote (`TestConsoleCloudSQLReadReplica`). Cascading and cross-region replicas: see the #1381 row below. High availability: see the #1408 row below. Legacy failover replicas and external-primary replicas are 501. See [cloudsql.md](cloudsql.md#read-replicas-1330). |

Also `gcloud sql instances create --database-version=POSTGRES_15` and `patch --database-version=POSTGRES_16` (`TestGcloudSQLDatabaseVersions`, gcloud 587.0.0), Terraform `database_version` `POSTGRES_14` changed to `POSTGRES_15` in place, plan clean (`TestTerraformSQLDatabaseVersion`), and the console's version picker and Upgrade (`TestConsoleCloudSQLVersionsAndUpgrade`). `maintenanceVersion` is not answered (it names Cloud SQL's own releases). An instance with replicas, or a replica, is 501 to upgrade. See [cloudsql.md](cloudsql.md#database-versions-and-major-version-upgrades-1381). |
| The Cloud SQL Admin API's cascading and cross-region read replicas: `sql.instances.insert` with `masterInstanceName` naming a replica, or a `region` other than the primary's | **Verified** | `TestCloudSQLCascadingAndCrossRegionReplicas` (#1381), official Go client `google.golang.org/api/sqladmin/v1` and `cloud.google.com/go/cloudsqlconn`, on both engines: a replica in `us-east1` of a `us-central1` primary answers that `region`, `gceZone` and connection name, and the connector reaches it by that name; a replica of it (PostgreSQL cascading streaming replication from the standby; MySQL GTID replication from the replica) receives a row written on the top primary and refuses writes; promoting the middle replica leaves its replica receiving the promoted one's writes; on PostgreSQL a fifth level of replicas is 400 (Cloud SQL allows four). Also `gcloud sql instances create --master-instance-name --region=europe-west1` (`TestGcloudSQLDatabaseVersions`) and the console's Create read replica on a replica (`TestConsoleCloudSQLReadReplica`). The region is reported, not a place: every server runs in the one cluster. See [cloudsql.md](cloudsql.md#cascading-and-cross-region-replicas-1381). |
| The Cloud SQL Admin API's backups: `sql.backupRuns.insert`, `sql.backupRuns.list`, `sql.backupRuns.get`, `sql.backupRuns.delete`, `sql.instances.restoreBackup`, `sql.instances.clone` | **Verified** | `TestCloudSQLBackups` (#1330), official Go client `google.golang.org/api/sqladmin/v1` with rows written and read through `cloud.google.com/go/cloudsqlconn`, on the servers `up` runs and on created instances, both engines: rows are written, `backupRuns.insert` takes a backup (`BACKUP_VOLUME`, the run `SUCCESSFUL`, listed and read back), the rows are changed, `restoreBackup` restores it and the original rows read back; on a created instance `clone` makes a new instance holding the same rows, and a clone to a point in time of an instance without point-in-time recovery is 400 (the next row). A backup is `pg_dump`/`mysqldump` of each application database run in the server's pod (the `cloudburrow snapshot` mechanism), kept in the instance directory; a restore drops and reloads the databases, and leaves users as they are. `settings.backupConfiguration` is recorded; an automated backup is taken at `startTime` only while CloudBurrow runs. Also through `gcloud sql backups create`, `list`, `restore` and `delete` (`TestGcloudSQLBackups`) and the console's Backups tab and Clone (`TestConsoleCloudSQLInstanceEditAndBackups`). See [cloudsql.md](cloudsql.md#backups-restores-and-clones-1330). |
| The Cloud SQL Admin API's point-in-time recovery: `sql.instances.clone` with `cloneContext.pointInTime`, `sql.projects.instances.getLatestRecoveryTime`, `settings.backupConfiguration.pointInTimeRecoveryEnabled` and `binaryLogEnabled` | **Verified** on created instances, both engines | `TestCloudSQLPointInTimeRecovery` (#1330), official Go client `google.golang.org/api/sqladmin/v1` with rows written and read through `cloud.google.com/go/cloudsqlconn`, on PostgreSQL 17 with `pointInTimeRecoveryEnabled` and MySQL 8.4 with `binaryLogEnabled`: `getLatestRecoveryTime` reports the window, rows are written, the server's time is noted, rows are changed and added, a clone to before the window is 400, and a clone to the noted time holds only the first rows while the source keeps every change. PostgreSQL archives its WAL and replays it to `recovery_target_time` from a `pg_basebackup` in a scratch server; MySQL loads a `mysqldump --source-data` base and replays its binary log with its own replication applier up to the first transaction committed after the time (the image has no `mysqlbinlog`); both to the microsecond. Also `gcloud sql instances create --enable-point-in-time-recovery` and `gcloud sql instances clone --point-in-time` (`TestGcloudSQLPointInTimeClone`) and the console's Point-in-time restore (`TestConsoleCloudSQLPointInTimeRestore`). The servers `up` runs keep no log: a clone of one to a time is 400. See [cloudsql.md](cloudsql.md#point-in-time-recovery-1330). |
| The Cloud SQL Admin API's log and backup retention: `settings.backupConfiguration.transactionLogRetentionDays`, `backupRetentionSettings`, and a backup whose base fails | **Verified** on created instances, both engines | `TestCloudSQLPointInTimeRetention` (#1330), official Go client `google.golang.org/api/sqladmin/v1` with rows written and read through `cloud.google.com/go/cloudsqlconn`, on PostgreSQL 17 and MySQL 8.4: `transactionLogRetentionDays` 8 on the Enterprise edition and `retainedBackups` 366 are 400, as Google documents the ranges (1 to 7 days on Enterprise, 35 on Enterprise Plus; 1 to 365 backups, `COUNT`); an instance with 1 day and 2 backups returns them; rows are written and a backup takes a second base; after `POST /cloudburrow/v1/clock:advance` ages the kept log by a day (a CloudBurrow extension, as Secret Manager's clock, #1278), `earliestRecoveryTime` has moved past the first rows, a clone to then is 400, and a clone to a time inside the window, recovered from the backup's base, holds exactly the rows written by then. The sweep drops the bases before the window's and the WAL (`pg_archivecleanup`) or binary logs (`PURGE BINARY LOGS TO`) only they needed. A backup whose base fails is `FAILED` with the error, and its operation fails (unit `TestPITRRetentionAndFailedBase`; not provoked through a real server). See [cloudsql.md](cloudsql.md#point-in-time-recovery-1330). |

A patch to `ZONAL` removes the standby, and a failover of a `ZONAL` instance is 400. MySQL falls back to asynchronous replication only after a commit has waited 4294967295 ms (about 49.7 days); between a promotion and the new standby streaming, commits do not wait (no failover is possible then). Also through `gcloud sql instances create --availability-type=regional`, `describe` and `gcloud sql instances failover` (`TestGcloudSQLHighAvailability`), Terraform's `google_sql_database_instance` with `availability_type = "REGIONAL"` and backups with point-in-time recovery, applied, planned clean, updated to `ZONAL` and back in place, each planned clean, and destroyed (`TestTerraformSQLHighAvailability`, hashicorp/google 8.4.0), both on PostgreSQL, and the console's **Zonal availability** on Create and Edit and **Failover** (`TestCloudSQLConsoleHighAvailability`, unit). Not built: automatic failover when the primary's pod fails, and carrying the old primary's point-in-time recovery log to the new one. See [cloudsql.md](cloudsql.md#high-availability-1408). |

TO STDOUT WITH (FORMAT csv)`, MySQL's `SELECT ... INTO OUTFILE` with Cloud SQL's `FIELDS TERMINATED BY ',' OPTIONALLY ENCLOSED BY '"' ESCAPED BY '"'`); `fieldsTerminatedBy`, `quoteCharacter`, `escapeCharacter` and, on MySQL, `linesTerminatedBy` take Google's hex character codes (`2C`). A `.gz` file is gzip. An import is an `IMPORT` operation that runs the file's statements (`psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1` as `importUser` or the default user; `mysql`) or loads its rows (`COPY ... FROM STDIN`, `LOAD DATA INFILE`) into `csvImportOptions.table` and `columns`. An export to a file that exists succeeds and its operation fails, as Google documents. `offload` is accepted and exports the same way (there is no serverless machine to offload to). `operations.cancel` stops a running import or export, whose operation ends `DONE` with the error `CANCEL_SUCCESSFUL`; any other operation, or one not in progress, answers 400 with Google's documented messages. 501: `BAK` and `TDE` files (SQL Server's), parallel imports and exports (`parallel`, `threads`: a directory of per-table files), `mysqlExportOptions.masterData`, and a `linesTerminatedBy` other than `0A` on PostgreSQL, whose `COPY` ends every row with a newline. `gcloud sql export sql/csv` and `gcloud sql import sql/csv` work. |

The servers take connections over the connector path, not direct TLS, so a client certificate is a record the server does not check. |
| The Cloud SQL Admin API: `sql.instances.listServerCas`, `sql.instances.addServerCa`, `sql.instances.rotateServerCa` | **Verified** | `TestSQLAdminServerCARotation` and `TestConsoleCloudSQLClientCertificates` (#1380): `addServerCa` makes an upcoming server CA beside the active one (replacing one added and never rotated in); `rotateServerCa` (with `nextVersion` its SHA-1 fingerprint, or none) makes it the CA `connectSettings` returns and the connector path signs its server and ephemeral certificates with, so the official connector connects after the rotation; the CA rotated out stays trusted for the client certificates it signed. `listServerCas` lists the active CA (`activeVersion`, its fingerprint), the upcoming one and the one rotated out. Rotating with no upcoming CA is 400. |
| The Cloud SQL Admin API: `sql.tiers.list`, `sql.flags.list` | **Verified** | `TestSQLAdminTiersAndFlags` and `TestGcloudSQLImportAndExport` (`gcloud sql tiers list`, `gcloud sql flags list`) (#1380): Google's documented lists, taken from its docs pages (`internal/service/sqladmin/flagsdata.go` names them): 27 tiers (shared-core, `db-custom-*` and `db-perf-optimized-N-*`, with their RAM; the disk quota Google documents for shared-core, 64 TB otherwise), and the supported flags of the versions served, `POSTGRES_13` (206), `POSTGRES_14` (213), `POSTGRES_15` (215), `POSTGRES_16` (215), `POSTGRES_17` (213), `POSTGRES_18` (225), `MYSQL_8_0` (173) and `MYSQL_8_4` (168) (#1381, from the version notes in Google's flag tables), each with its type, allowed values or range, and whether it needs a restart, filtered by `databaseVersion`; another Cloud SQL version lists none. |
| Google-published component | **No** | The only one here that is not. Google publishes no Cloud SQL emulator — `gcloud emulators` ships firestore and spanner, and the sole Cloud SQL component is `cloud-sql-proxy`, which connects to a real instance in GCP. |

An application that talks SQL works. Since #1301 an application or tool that lists instances, or
creates databases and users through the Cloud SQL Admin API, works too, and since #1330 so does
one that creates instances or connects through the Cloud SQL Go connector, or uses backups, read
replicas and point-in-time recovery, and since #1408 high availability (`REGIONAL`, `instances.failover`);
IAM database authentication, legacy failover replicas and `pointInTimeRestore` do not. See [cloudsql.md](cloudsql.md) and
[#121](https://github.com/cloudburrow/cloudburrow/issues/121).

### Memorystore is not an emulator

| Capability | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| A real Redis-compatible server, locally | **Verified** | `TestMemorystoreDataPlane` (#296), with `github.com/redis/go-redis/v9` and nothing of CloudBurrow's: SET/GET, MULTI/EXEC, PUBLISH/SUBSCRIBE and Lua EVAL against the host endpoint, and GET from a pod through `memorystore.cloudburrow.svc.cluster.local:6379`. Valkey 8.1.10, digest-pinned. The host address comes from `REDIS_HOST`/`REDIS_PORT` as `cloudburrow env` exports them. |
| Durability | **Verified, measured** | CI stops and starts the persistent compat instance and `TestMemorystoreAcrossRestart` reads back a key written before the stop; brought up again in `--mode ephemeral`, the same test finds no key. This evidence tolerates one retry: `TestMemorystoreAcrossRestart` is on CI's [retry-once list](#retried-once). Persistent mode is an append-only file on a PVC, fsynced every second, so up to a second of writes can be lost on a crash; ephemeral mode writes nothing to disk. |
| The Memorystore admin API (`redis.googleapis.com`) | **Partial** | Served since #1302: see [Memorystore for Redis](#memorystore-for-redis--googlecloudredisv1). The instance `up` runs is described; instances are created, resized and deleted, each a Valkey server of its own, exported to and imported from Cloud Storage as RDB files, with RDB persistence (#1384); Upgrade, Failover and maintenance are 501. |
| Console screen | **Verified** | The Memorystore page (#1302) lists the instances through the admin API's `ListInstances`, offers **Flush** (FLUSHALL, confirmed) on the instance `up` runs (`TestConsoleMemorystoreFlush`), and **Create instance**, **Edit** and **Delete** through `CreateInstance`, `UpdateInstance` and `DeleteInstance`, with the AUTH string on an instance's page (`TestConsoleMemorystoreCreateEditDelete`). Recorded in [console-parity.md](console-parity.md) §3. |
| Google-published component | **No** | Google publishes no Memorystore emulator. Valkey is the server Memorystore for Valkey runs; Memorystore for Redis runs Redis, with which Valkey is protocol-compatible. |
| Authentication | **None** on the server `up` runs; **AUTH** on a created instance with `auth_enabled` | No password on the server `up` runs, as for Cloud SQL: nothing in CloudBurrow authenticates a request, and the host endpoint is loopback only; an application that sends `AUTH` to it gets an error. An instance created with `auth_enabled` runs with `--requirepass` set to a generated string (a UUID, as Google's are), which `GetInstanceAuthString` returns; without it a client gets NOAUTH (`TestMemorystoreCreateConnectUpdateDelete`). The string is in the server's Deployment arguments in the cluster. |

An application that talks RESP works. An application that calls the Memorystore admin API can
list and describe the instance `up` runs, and create, resize and delete BASIC instances of its
own, each a real Valkey server. See [memorystore.md](memorystore.md) and
[#296](https://github.com/cloudburrow/cloudburrow/issues/296).

**Bigtable starts without the network.** Its emulator is in the pinned Cloud SDK emulators image
and is the container's command; nothing is installed when the container starts (#611, #604).

Not covered, and not claimed: Firestore
indexes and security rules, Datastore composite indexes, Spanner dialects other than
GoogleSQL, and backup/restore for any of them.

### Host endpoints survive a backend restart

| Capability | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Advertised host port after a pod restart | **Verified** | `TestHostEndpointSurvivesABackendRestart` restarts the pod and requires the printed address to both accept a connection **and carry a request**; this evidence tolerates one retry, since the test is on CI's [retry-once list](#retried-once). Each tunnel binds a pod the forwarder chooses itself: the newest one that is Ready and **not being deleted**. `kubectl port-forward svc/…` could bind a pod that was terminating but still Ready during a rollout, such as `up --mode ephemeral` replacing a persistent pod, and connections through it hung (#381). |

This was broken until the restart criterion exposed it: the forwarder started `kubectl
port-forward` once and watched nothing, so a crash, an OOM kill, an eviction or a rollout left
the advertised endpoint dead for the life of the instance, while the pod was `Running`, the
service existed, and the startup banner still printed the address. Worse than a refusal: the
port still **accepted connections** and carried nothing, so a client's `connect()` succeeded
and every request timed out.

The tunnel is supervised and re-established on the **same** host port — the address has
already been printed, may be in an application's configuration, and for storage is baked into
the backend's advertised download URL, so reconnecting elsewhere would be a different kind of
broken. `Restarts()` counts re-establishments, because surviving a restart and never noticing
one are different states.

**Why it still flaked in CI (#526), measured:** `kubectl port-forward` does **not** exit when
its pod is deleted while the tunnel is idle. It keeps listening, fails the *next* connection's
stream, and exits only then. A supervisor that watched only for the process exiting therefore
kept a dead tunnel until a client tripped over it, and on a loaded runner the relaunch that
followed could bind the Service, resolving to whichever pod kubectl found, Ready or not.
Three failed CI runs showed the shape: the emulator up within a second of the restart, every
forwarder reporting its process alive, and clients timing out for minutes reading a server
preface that never came. Now the supervisor **watches the bound pod** and replaces the tunnel
within seconds of the pod going, **binds only a Ready, non-terminating pod** when it
re-establishes (never the Service), and counts a tunnel as up only once a probe connection
through it is **carried**, not merely accepted, using kubectl's own stream errors as the
signal. Each exit and re-establishment is logged, so a diagnose bundle says what the tunnel
did. In-process: `TestATunnelWhosePodIsGoneIsReplacedWithoutAClient`,
`TestRelaunchWaitsForAReadyPodInsteadOfTheService`, `TestALaunchWhoseStreamFailsIsRetried`,
against a fake kubectl.

A function is built as Google builds a 2nd-gen one: a Cloud Build build of `build_config.source.storage_source` with Google's buildpacks (SubmitBuild's buildpacks path, `GOOGLE_RUNTIME` set from `build_config.runtime`, `entry_point` the function target, `build_config.environment_variables` the build's), then a Cloud Run service of the function's ID running the image, named in `service_config.service` and `url`. `TestFunctionsAPI` (ungated, the official `functions/apiv2` client over gRPC): `ListRuntimes`; `GenerateUploadUrl` returns a URL on the Run port that takes an unauthenticated PUT of the zip, written to `gcf-v2-uploads-{project number}-{region}` in the instance's Cloud Storage, and `GenerateDownloadUrl` reads it back; a create is `DEPLOYING` behind an operation with `OperationMetadata` (`target`, `CREATE_FUNCTION`, build and service stages), `ALREADY_EXISTS` a second time; a source that does not build fails the operation (`Build failed: …`) and leaves the function `FAILED` with a state message; `service_config` keeps memory, timeout, environment, the service account (stored; the revision runs as the host) and max/min instances, defaulted as Google does (256M, 60s, 100 instances, the compute default account); get, list, an update of the description (which runs nothing) and delete. `TestFunctionsAPIBuildsAndServes`, gated as the Functions tests are (amd64 nodes, pack) and **not yet run**: `testdata/function` PUT to an upload URL, created as `go123`, `ACTIVE` with its url and service, which answers the greeting; an update of `service_config.environment_variables` rolls out a new revision of the same build; delete removes the service. An unknown runtime is `INVALID_ARGUMENT`; `ListFunctions` `filter`, `order_by` and `page_token`, `GetFunction` `revision`, GEN_1, `repo_source`, `git_uri`, worker pools, `docker_repository`, a build service account, VPC connectors, secrets, KMS and binary authorization are **`UNIMPLEMENTED`**. Functions are kept in memory. Console: Cloud Functions page. |
| Cloud Functions v2 IAM (`functions.getIamPolicy`, `setIamPolicy`, `testIamPermissions`) | **Verified**, *stored, not enforced* | `TestFunctionsAPI`: a policy set on a function is read back with its binding; `TestIamPermissions` returns every permission asked. ADR-0006: nothing consults it, so `allUsers` as invoker changes nothing here. |
| Cloud Functions v2 `eventTrigger` (Pub/Sub and Cloud Storage) | **Verified**, *locally delivered* | `TestFunctionsEventTriggers` (#1414), through the official Functions, Pub/Sub and Storage clients on an instance with `--services run,storage,pubsub`, each function serving `testdata/eventprobe`, which records what it is sent. The trigger is made once the service is deployed, as Eventarc makes a 2nd-gen function's: `event_trigger.trigger` reads `projects/*/locations/{trigger_region}/triggers/{function}-{6 digits}`, `trigger_region` defaults to the function's, `service_account_email` to the function's (the default compute account) and `retry_policy` to `RETRY_POLICY_DO_NOT_RETRY`. **`google.cloud.pubsub.topic.v1.messagePublished`**: a push subscription `eventarc-{region}-{trigger}-sub-{NNN}` on `pubsub_topic`, labelled `goog-managed-by: eventarc` (the label is UNVERIFIED against Google), with a 600-second ack deadline, a day's retention and a 10 to 600 second backoff; a published message reaches the function as a binary-mode CloudEvent with `ce-id` (the message ID), `ce-source` `//pubsub.googleapis.com/{topic}`, `ce-type`, `ce-specversion` 1.0, `ce-time` (the publish time) and Google's `MessagePublishedData` JSON (`message`, with both spellings of its ID and time, and `subscription`). **`google.cloud.storage.object.v1.finalized`, `deleted`, `archived`, `metadataUpdated`** with an `event_filters` `bucket`: a topic `eventarc-{region}-{trigger}-{NNN}`, the bucket's `JSON_API_V1` notification for the matching event type on it, and a push subscription on that topic; an upload reaches the function with `ce-subject` `objects/{name}`, `ce-source` `//storage.googleapis.com/projects/_/buckets/{bucket}`, the `ce-bucket` extension, `ce-time` the notification's event time and the object resource as the data (only finalized is exercised by the test; the other three differ only in the notification's event type). Each delivery carries `Authorization: Bearer` with an ID token for the trigger's account, audience the service URL, minted by the instance (see Cloud Tasks' `oidcToken` for how it differs from Google's). Deleting the function removes the subscription, notification and topic its trigger made, and leaves the user's topic. Unit `TestStorageTriggerDeliversAndTearsDown`, `TestPubSubPushBecomesMessagePublishedCloudEvent`, `TestStorageNotificationBecomesObjectCloudEvent`, `TestEventTriggersAreChecked`. **What differs from Google:** the subscription pushes to the Run port (`/cloudburrow/eventarc/push/{trigger}` at its `cloudburrow-host` name), not to the service: this process converts the push and POSTs the CloudEvent to the ingress on this machine, so it needs a published ingress port; a failed delivery (not 102, 200, 201, 202 or 204) is answered back to Pub/Sub and retried under `RETRY_POLICY_RETRY`, and acknowledged and dropped under `DO_NOT_RETRY`; `ce-id` of a Storage event is the Pub/Sub message ID; no `eventarc.googleapis.com` API is served, so the trigger can be named but not read; triggers are kept in memory with the functions. **`UNIMPLEMENTED`**: other event types (audit logs, Firestore, custom channels), `channel`, `service`, filters other than an exact `bucket`, and a trigger on an instance without Pub/Sub (`TestFunctionsAPI` asserts an audit log trigger is refused naming the event type). `TestGcloudFunctionsEventTriggers` (#1414), the pinned gcloud through `gcloud-setup`, egress to Google blocked, ungated: `functions deploy --gen2 --trigger-topic=T --retry --trigger-service-account=SA` and `--trigger-event-filters=type=google.cloud.storage.object.v1.finalized --trigger-event-filters=bucket=B` of a `gs://` source that is not a zip fail with this instance's build error, and `describe` shows the `eventTrigger` gcloud sent (event type, `pubsubTopic` in gcloud's project, the bucket filter, retry policy, account, region); a redeploy with `--no-retry`, an `UpdateFunction` whose `updateMask` mixes snake_case paths with `eventTrigger.retryPolicy`, as gcloud sends it, changes only the retry policy. Gated as the Functions tests are, and **not yet run**: `TestFunctionsEventTriggerBuilds` builds `testdata/function`'s `Event` entry point (the Functions Framework CloudEvent function) with Google's builder under a Pub/Sub and a Cloud Storage trigger, and a publish and an upload reach it, read back from its printed line through Cloud Logging; `TestGcloudFunctionsEventTriggers`' gated half does the same through `gcloud functions deploy --gen2`, with `describe` naming the trigger. |
| `gcloud functions` (`--gen2`) | **Verified** (`list --v2`, `describe`, `delete`; `deploy` gated) | `TestGcloudFunctions`, the pinned gcloud through `gcloud-setup`'s `cloudfunctions` override, egress to Google blocked: `functions list --v2`, `describe --gen2` and `delete --gen2` of a function the client created; `deploy --runtime=go999` is refused by gcloud from this instance's `ListRuntimes`. `deploy --gen2` of `testdata/function` (upload URL, create, operation, the url answering) is gated as the Functions tests are and **not yet run**. |
| Node.js functions | **Verified** | `TestFunctionsNodejsBuiltWithBuildpacks` (#1303) builds `testdata/function-nodejs` (`package.json`, its lockfile and `index.js` on `@google-cloud/functions-framework` 5.0.5) with the pinned builder, which detects Node.js from `package.json`, deploys `Hello` (`http`) and `Event` (`cloudevent`) through the official Cloud Run v2 client, and asserts the greeting, a body-less 200 and the logged CloudEvent. No 400 is asserted for a request without `ce-*` headers: the Node.js framework hands such a body to the function as a structured-mode event. Gated; Verified by a dated run (2026-10-15, [run 38805202491](https://github.com/cloudburrow/cloudburrow/actions/runs/38805202491), amd64; [What CI does not run](#what-ci-does-not-run-and-why)). |
| Python functions | **Verified** | `TestFunctionsPythonBuiltWithBuildpacks` (#1303) builds `testdata/function-python` (`requirements.txt` pinning `functions-framework==3.10.2`, `main.py`) with the pinned builder, which detects Python from `requirements.txt`, deploys `hello` (`http`) and `event` (`cloudevent`), and asserts the same as the Node.js test plus the framework's HTTP 400 for a request that is not a CloudEvent. Gated; Verified by the same dated run (2026-10-15, run 38805202491). |
| Runtime selection | **Implemented** | `buildpacks.Detect`, run before pack: `GOOGLE_RUNTIME` in the build's environment (SubmitBuild's `buildpack_build.environment_variables`) wins and reaches pack unchanged; otherwise the builder detects from the source's markers (`go.mod`, `package.json`, `requirements.txt`, `pyproject.toml`, `setup.py`, `pom.xml`, `build.gradle`, `Gemfile`, `composer.json`, then `.go`, `.js`, `.py`, `.jar`, `.rb`, `.php`, `.csproj` sources). CloudBurrow never forces a runtime, so a source matching several is built as the builder's order decides; a source with none is refused before pack runs (`build failed: no runtime detected`, naming the files and `GOOGLE_RUNTIME`), and a failed build names the runtime it was built as. Unit: `TestDetect*`, `TestBuildRefusesASourceWithNoRuntime`, `TestBuildFailureNamesTheRuntime`. `buildpack_build.runtime` stays **`UNIMPLEMENTED`**. |
| Java, Ruby, PHP and .NET functions | **Verified** | #1319: `TestFunctionsJavaBuiltWithBuildpacks` builds `testdata/function-java` (a Maven `pom.xml` on `functions-framework-api` 1.1.4, `functions.Hello` and `functions.Event`), `TestFunctionsRubyBuiltWithBuildpacks` `testdata/function-ruby` (a `Gemfile` and its lockfile pinning `functions_framework` 1.7.0, `app.rb`), `TestFunctionsPHPBuiltWithBuildpacks` `testdata/function-php` (`composer.json` pinning `google/cloud-functions-framework` 1.4.3, `index.php`, which logs to stderr since its standard output is the response) and `TestFunctionsDotnetBuiltWithBuildpacks` `testdata/function-dotnet` (`Function.csproj` on `Google.Cloud.Functions.Hosting` 3.0.1 for net8.0, `Fixture.Hello` and `Fixture.Event`), each with the pinned builder, which detects the language from that manifest (for the PHP function, Google's PHP functions builder, since the general builder has no PHP Functions Framework buildpack), and assert what the Node.js test does: the greeting, a body-less 200 and the logged CloudEvent; no 400 is asserted, since nothing has measured these frameworks' answer to a request that is not a CloudEvent. Gated; Verified by a dated run (2026-10-15, [run 38805202491](https://github.com/cloudburrow/cloudburrow/actions/runs/38805202491) of `functions.yml`, amd64). The builder makes amd64 images only, so what is checked on every change is that `buildpacks.Detect` names each fixture's language from its manifest (`TestDetectTheFunctionFixtures`). |
| Native amd64 build host | **Verified** | `TestFunctionsFrameworkBuiltWithBuildpacks` runs only when the cluster nodes are amd64, since the builder emits amd64 images; Verified by the dated CI run (2026-09-27, run 36357529139, `ubuntu-latest` amd64). Gated; no merge runs it. The emulated arm64 build was only tried by hand. |

**The builder is `linux/amd64` only.** On arm64 it runs under emulation and emits an amd64
image, which needs an amd64-capable node. CloudBurrow reports this rather than letting it
surface as a scheduling failure.

## Local AI

**Text generation works**, on a runtime CloudBurrow builds from Google's source. See
[local-ai.md](local-ai.md), including §4 — which corrects this page's previous conclusion.

**Not re-run in CI.** The model download and CPU inference are too heavy for per-PR CI, so the
Verified rows in this section and in Vertex AI generation come from runs on a developer machine:
generation on 2026-09-21, embeddings on 2026-10-15 and again on 2026-10-16 (see
[What CI does not run](#what-ci-does-not-run-and-why)).

**Two embedding routes, one served.** The official LiteRT route (Google's
`embedding_litert_lm_main` on Google's EmbeddingGemma artifacts) is blocked on the model export,
so it serves nothing. Embeddings are served from a **community** ONNX conversion on ONNX Runtime
instead. The rows below name the route each one is about.

| Capability | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Model catalogue with verified provenance | **Verified** | Publisher recorded per artifact; a community conversion is never reported as Google-published. |
| Gated-artifact handling | **Verified** | Refused without credentials, with an actionable message. |
| Disk preflight, checksum verification, atomic cache, recovery | **Verified** | `internal/localai` |
| **Linux generation runtime** | **Verified** | `//runtime/engine:litert_lm_main` built from source at commit `02e5030` and run **from the shipped image**: **78.43 tok/s prefill, 31.98 tok/s decode, 0.39 s to first token** over a 144-token generation, CPU backend, warm cache. No LiteRT-LM release publishes a Linux artifact; Linux is nevertheless a documented, supported build target, and the gap is packaging rather than capability. |
| **Linux LiteRT embedding runtime** | **Runs; no model to run** | `//runtime/engine:embedding_litert_lm_main` builds, ships in the runtime image, loads models and initialises its engine. Every obtainable model is then rejected — see [embeddings.md](embeddings.md). |
| **Text generation** | **Verified** | On `litert-community/gemma-4-E2B-it.litertlm` (2.59 GB, ungated). |
| **A Google-published runnable model** | **Not available** | Every one is `gated: manual`. The model that works is a **community** conversion and is labelled as one everywhere it appears. |
| **Embeddings on the LiteRT runtime (official artifacts)** | **Blocked on the model export, not the runtime and not access** | Embeddings are served by the community ONNX route instead (next row); this row is about the LiteRT route alone. The earlier statement — *every embedding artifact is gated* — was **wrong**: three are ungated. They fail for another reason. One ships with no tokenizer at all; rebuilt correctly with Google's own `litert-lm-builder` it reaches `Input tensor bytes must be 4 but got 2048`, as does an independent bundle from a different publisher. The conversions export a fixed `[1,512]` encoder signature and the engine requires a dynamic one. No flag bridges it. See [embeddings.md](embeddings.md). |
| **Embeddings (community ONNX int8 EmbeddingGemma)** | **Verified** (measured 2026-10-15) | Maintainer decision 2026-09-28 (#41): `embeddinggemma-300m-onnx-community`, onnx-community's ONNX int8 conversion of EmbeddingGemma — **NOT an official Google artifact**, and labelled so in the API response (`modelDisplayName`, `X-CloudBurrow-Model-Provenance`), the console and the catalogue. Pinned to `onnx-community/embeddinggemma-300m-ONNX` revision `5090578d`, each file by SHA-256, licence `gemma`, fetched over HTTPS by `up -local-ai-embeddings`. Runs on ONNX Runtime only in a `-tags onnx` build; the default build answers every `:predict` 501. **Measured against the real model** (#41) on an Apple M4 Max (48 GB, macOS 27.0.1, darwin/arm64), `make onnx-compile`'s `bin/cloudburrow-onnx` with ONNX Runtime 1.29.0 (the official `onnxruntime-osx-arm64-1.29.0.tgz` release, checked by SHA-256; the version `onnxruntime_go` v1.36.0's headers name) and libtokenizers v1.27.0: `up -local-ai-embeddings` fetched and verified the pinned files; 768, 512, 256 and 128 dimensions, every value finite, each a unit vector, the smaller sizes the renormalised prefix of 768 (cosine ≥ 0.9999); task types change the vector and an unknown one is 400; a sourdough-bread query scored 0.6108 against a bread-making passage and 0.0928 against an interest-rate one. An 11-token input took 37 ms per request (median of 10, warm); the whole CLI process was 1.3 GB resident. `TestEmbeddingGemmaThroughTheOfficialSDK`, official `google.golang.org/genai` on its Vertex AI backend, run where `CLOUDBURROW_TEST_EMBEDDINGS` names such an instance's local AI endpoint. The official LiteRT artifacts remain blocked as described in [embeddings.md](embeddings.md). |
| Output quality | **Not claimed** | The measured run answered a factual question wrongly. That is a small quantised model's quality; CloudBurrow does not present model output as correct. |
| Benchmarks | **Measured, single sample** | One run on one machine (Apple M4 Max, arm64, CPU, container). Not a benchmark, and no comparison is drawn from them. Two conditions change them substantially: a **cold** XNNPACK cache raises init from 0.31 s to 3.27 s, and a **short** answer collapses decode speed (6.89 tok/s over two tokens on the same binary) because the first token's fixed cost is averaged over the generation. |
| Pinned artifact checksums | **Absent** for the Google artifacts · **Verified** for the community ONNX embedding files | The Google artifacts are gated, so they could not be downloaded and hashed; the status reports the absence rather than implying verification. The three files of `embeddinggemma-300m-onnx-community` are pinned by SHA-256 in `internal/localai/catalog.go` and verified before use: the files `up -local-ai-embeddings` fetched on 2026-10-16 hash to those pins (`shasum -a 256`). |
| Runtime distribution | **Published per release; not yet exercised by one** | Each release builds `deploy/litert-lm/Dockerfile` natively for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64, pushes `ghcr.io/cloudburrow/litert-lm:<tag>`, attests the index, and records its digest in the release notes. A release CLI defaults `--local-ai-image` to that digest and pulls it on first use; a checkout build defaults to `cloudburrow/litert-lm:local` from `make litert-lm`, never pulled (#602). No release has run this job yet, so no published digest exists. Locally, the Dockerfile builds it: **6m17s measured** from a cold cache on an M4 Max with 16 CPUs, once, producing a 274 MB image. Debian 13 is the base because Abseil needs C++20 `<source_location>`, which Debian 12's default clang 14 lacks. |
| Runtime image completeness | **Verified** | The image is run, not merely built. `litert_lm_main` links `libGemmaModelConstraintProvider.so` — shipped prebuilt upstream, found via a `RUNPATH` into Bazel's output tree — so a multi-stage build that copies only the binary produces an image that builds cleanly and fails on first run. The prebuilt libraries are staged and registered with `ldconfig`. |
| Catalogue artifact filenames | **Verified against the live API** | `TestCatalogArtifactsExistUpstream` (tag `upstream`) lists each repository and asserts the named file is in it, and HEADs the resolve URL for entries marked ungated. It was written after the community entry was found naming `gemma-4-E2B-it-int4.litertlm`, a filename inferred from the `google/` repositories' convention, which returns **404**. |

## Vertex AI generation (local)

A **subset** of `generateContent`, served by the runtime CloudBurrow builds. Not a Vertex
emulator and not a Gemini replica. See [generation.md](generation.md) for the exact surface.

| Capability | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `generateContent` through the official SDK | **Verified** | `TestRealGenerationThroughTheOfficialSDK`, `google.golang.org/genai` v1.71.0 pointed at a local endpoint, real runtime, real model. |
| `streamGenerateContent` (SSE) | **Verified** | 12 events over 741 ms through the SDK's own stream iterator. A unit test additionally asserts the first event arrives *while generation is still running*, so streaming cannot regress into buffering. |
| Both SDK path shapes | **Verified** | Vertex `/v1beta1/projects/{p}/locations/{l}/publishers/google/models/{m}:verb` and Gemini-API `/v1beta/models/{m}:verb`, taken from what the SDK actually sends. |
| No silent model substitution | **Verified** | A request for another model returns 404 naming what is served; `modelVersion` reports what ran; aliases must be configured by hand. |
| Generation options | **None supported** | Every one is refused with a message naming it. `maxOutputTokens` is refused on measurement: the runtime accepts it and ignores it — 309 decoded tokens at limits of 8, 40 and unset. |
| Tools, safety settings, multimodal input, multi-turn, `countTokens` | **Refused** | Each returns an error rather than being ignored. `safetySettings` in particular: **no filtering happens here**, so accepting the field would imply it does. |
| Token accounting | **Absent** for generation · **Verified** for embeddings | `generateContent` and `streamGenerateContent` never emit `usageMetadata`: the LiteRT runtime reports no token count, and none is estimated. The embedding model does count, with its own tokenizer: `EmbedContent` (gRPC and REST `:embedContent`) answers `usage_metadata.prompt_token_count` and `total_token_count`, and text-embedding `:predict` answers `statistics.token_count`. Measured 2026-10-16, `bin/cloudburrow-onnx` with ONNX Runtime 1.29.0 on darwin/arm64: "How do I bake sourdough bread?" counted 16 tokens through both; `TestEmbedContentThroughThePredictionClient` asserts a positive count. |
| Prompt/output separation | **Verified** | The runtime echoes the prompt before generating, and echoes a multi-line prompt across lines, so forwarding from the marker returned the caller's own prompt as generated text. The echo is now skipped by matching rather than counting, which stays correct if a future runtime stops echoing. Covered against a simulated runtime in both directions and against the real one by `TestRealMultiLinePromptIsNotEchoedBack`. |
| Cancellation | **Verified** | A cancelled request kills the runtime container by name. Found by testing: killing the `docker run` client left the container generating, because it is a client for work in the daemon and the runtime ignores `SIGTERM`. |
| Output quality, safety, or equivalence to Gemini | **Not claimed** | No test asserts what the model says. |
| Embeddings from an official LiteRT artifact | **Blocked on the model export** | The LiteRT route serves nothing. See [embeddings.md](embeddings.md): ungated artifacts do exist, and the runtime rejects them. Embeddings are served from the community ONNX conversion (next row). |
| Text-embedding `:predict` subset | **Verified** (measured 2026-10-15) | `POST /v1` (and `/v1beta1`) `/projects/{p}/locations/{l}/publishers/google/models/embeddinggemma-300m-onnx-community:predict` only: `instances[].content`, `task_type` (EmbeddingGemma's prompt prefixes), `title`; `parameters.autoTruncate`, `outputDimensionality` (768/512/256/128, truncated and renormalised). Any other model is 404, never substituted. Response `predictions[].embeddings.values` and `statistics`. Unit-tested with a fake runtime (`TestPredictServesOnlyTheCommunityIdentity`), and run against the real model through the official `google.golang.org/genai` SDK (Vertex AI backend, `Models.EmbedContent`, which sends `:predict` for a model that is not Gemini) by `TestEmbeddingGemmaThroughTheOfficialSDK` (#41; gated on `CLOUDBURROW_TEST_EMBEDDINGS`; numbers and machine in the Embeddings row above). Over gRPC, `cloud.google.com/go/aiplatform`'s `PredictionClient` reaches the same model through `Predict` (#1193) and `EmbedContent` (#1244), and REST `:embedContent` is served too; see the PredictionService table below. The genai SDK cannot send `autoTruncate: false` (its field is `omitempty`), so that refusal is unit-tested only. A **community conversion, not an official Google artifact**. Console: Vertex AI → Embeddings. |

### Console playground

| Capability | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Real inference from the browser | **Verified** | Driven through Chromium against the real runtime; 12 lines generated, streamed. |

The same operations are `/admin/local-models` on the control port, with the admin token. `TestConsoleLocalModelsLoadEmbedUnload` (the genai SDK refused after the console's Unload, the admin API's Load seen by the console, the console's `:embedContent` vector the SDK's) and `TestConsoleLocalModelsUnloadDeleteDownloadLoad` pass against an ONNX build; see [embeddings.md](embeddings.md). Custom prediction has its own page; see [Vertex AI custom prediction](#vertex-ai-custom-prediction). |
